Content:
Consider the standard basis [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square spanned by these two vectors.

Content:
Let's define a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf R] by its standard matrix [MATH: R,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [\cos 30^{∘}|− \sin 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}|\cos 30^{∘}]]

Content:
We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf{R}] by computing the matrix products, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: i^{′}|= R(i) = [\cos 30^{∘}|− \sin 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}|\cos 30^{∘}][1; 0] = [\cos 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}]; j^{′}|= R(j) = [\cos 30^{∘}|− \sin 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}|\cos 30^{∘}][0; 1] = [− \sin 30^{∘}; \cos 30^{∘}]]

Content:
Plotting the vectors [MATH: \mathbf i] and [MATH: \mathbf j] and their images [MATH: \mathbf i'] and [MATH: \mathbf j',] we obtain the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b191cb068776f81a39fb9de5734cb043]

Content:
We see that the transformation [MATH: \mathbf R] represented by the matrix [MATH: R] defines a counterclockwise rotation of [MATH: 30^\circ] about the origin.

Content:
As usual, we typically refer to rotations in the counterclockwise sense. However, in this case, the transformation [MATH: \mathbf R] can also be considered a rotation of [MATH: 360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ] clockwise about the origin.

sections.readable_text: The vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}=\langle -5,4 \rangle] is rotated [MATH: 135^{\circ}] counterclockwise about the origin. Find the image of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] under this rotation.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A rotation of [MATH: 135^{\circ}] counterclockwise about the origin is represented by the matrix [MATH: [\cos (135^{∘})|− \sin (135^{∘}); \sin (135^{∘})|\cos (135^{∘})]]

To find the image [MATH: \mathbf{v}'] under the action of the matrix [MATH: R_{135^{\circ}}], we compute the matrix product, as follows: [MATH: v^{′}|= R_{135^{∘}} ⋅ v; = [− (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2))][− 5; 4]; = [(1)/(sqrt(2)); − (9)/(sqrt(2))]]

Therefore, the image is [MATH: \mathbf{v}'=\left\langle \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, -\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{2}} \right\rangle.]

items.title: Interpreting a Given Matrix as a Rotation

sections.normalized_html:
What is the geometrical interpretation of the transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: A] given below?

[MATH: [− (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2))]]
sections.readable_text:
What is the geometrical interpretation of the transformation represented by the matrix [MATH: A] given below?

[MATH: [− (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2))]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The rotation matrix [MATH: R_\theta] represents a rotation of angle [MATH: \theta] counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

[MATH: [\cos θ|− \sin θ; \sin θ|\cos θ]]

Comparing [MATH: A] with the rotation matrix, we have

[MATH: {\sin θ = (1)/(sqrt(2)); \cos θ = − (1)/(sqrt(2)).]

Since [MATH: \sin \theta] is positive and [MATH: \cos \theta] is negative, we must have [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \pi.]

Dividing the first equation by the second gives [MATH: \tan \theta = -1.]

The principal value [MATH: \theta_1] is

[MATH: \theta_1 = \arctan (-1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4},]

but this is outside the range [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \pi.] To find a value in the required range, we add [MATH: \pi{:}]

[MATH: \theta = \theta_1 + \pi = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}]

Therefore, [MATH: A] represents a rotation of [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{4}] radians counterclockwise about the origin.

Note that this is also equivalent to a clockwise rotation with an angle of rotation given by

[MATH: 2\pi - \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}.]

sections.normalized_html:
A triangle [MATH: S] has vertices at [MATH: (1,1), (3,4), (5,8).] Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of [MATH: S',] the image of [MATH: S] under a counterclockwise rotation of [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{3}] radians about the origin?

  1. [MATH: \left(1,-3\right)]

  2. [MATH: \big(0,\sqrt{3}\big)]

  3. [MATH: \left(\dfrac{5-8\sqrt{3}}{2},\dfrac{8+5\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)]
sections.readable_text:
A triangle [MATH: S] has vertices at [MATH: (1,1), (3,4), (5,8).] Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of [MATH: S',] the image of [MATH: S] under a counterclockwise rotation of [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{3}] radians about the origin?

1. [MATH: \left(1,-3\right)]
2. [MATH: \big(0,\sqrt{3}\big)]
3. [MATH: \left(\dfrac{5-8\sqrt{3}}{2},\dfrac{8+5\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The rotation matrix [MATH: R_\theta] represents a rotation of angle [MATH: \theta] counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

[MATH: [\cos θ|− \sin θ; \sin θ|\cos θ]]

Substituting [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}] into the above, we have

[MATH: R|= [\cos ((π)/(3))|− \sin ((π)/(3)); \sin ((π)/(3))|\cos ((π)/(3))]; = [(1)/(2)|− (sqrt(3))/(2); (sqrt(3))/(2)|(1)/(2)]; = (1)/(2)[1|− sqrt(3); sqrt(3)|1].]

To find the image of [MATH: S] under the transformation, we first create a matrix [MATH: X] containing all of the vertices of [MATH: S\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: [1|3|5; 1|4|8]]

Now, we compute the image of [MATH: X] under the rotation [MATH: \mathbf{R}] by calculating the matrix product [MATH: RX\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: RX|= (1)/(2)[1|− sqrt(3); sqrt(3)|1][1|3|5; 1|4|8]; = (1)/(2)[1 − sqrt(3)|3 − 4sqrt(3)|5 − 8sqrt(3); 1 + sqrt(3)|4 + 3sqrt(3)|8 + 5sqrt(3)]; = [(1 − sqrt(3))/(2)|(3 − 4sqrt(3))/(2)|(5 − 8sqrt(3))/(2); (1 + sqrt(3))/(2)|(4 + 3sqrt(3))/(2)|(8 + 5sqrt(3))/(2)]] Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of [MATH: S'] are [MATH: \left(\dfrac{1-\sqrt{3}}{2},\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}\right), \quad \left(\dfrac{3-4\sqrt{3}}{2},\dfrac{4+3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right),\quad \left(\dfrac{5-8\sqrt{3}}{2},\dfrac{8+5\sqrt{3}}{2}\right).] So, the correct answer is "III only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the standard basis [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \big\}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square spanned by these two vectors.

Content:
Let's define a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf R] by its standard matrix [MATH: R,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [\cos 30^{∘}|− \sin 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}|\cos 30^{∘}]]

Content:
We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: \mathbf{R}] by computing the matrix products, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: i^{′}|= R(i) = [\cos 30^{∘}|− \sin 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}|\cos 30^{∘}][1; 0] = [\cos 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}]; j^{′}|= R(j) = [\cos 30^{∘}|− \sin 30^{∘}; \sin 30^{∘}|\cos 30^{∘}][0; 1] = [− \sin 30^{∘}; \cos 30^{∘}]]

Content:
Plotting the vectors [MATH: \mathbf i] and [MATH: \mathbf j] and their images [MATH: \mathbf i'] and [MATH: \mathbf j',] we obtain the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b191cb068776f81a39fb9de5734cb043]

Content:
We see that the transformation [MATH: \mathbf R] represented by the matrix [MATH: R] defines a counterclockwise rotation of [MATH: 30^\circ] about the origin.

Content:
As usual, we typically refer to rotations in the counterclockwise sense. However, in this case, the transformation [MATH: \mathbf R] can also be considered a rotation of [MATH: 360^\circ-30^\circ=330^\circ] clockwise about the origin.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: General Rotation Matrix

Content:
The matrix [MATH: R_\theta,] given by
[MATH: [\cos θ|− \sin θ; \sin θ|\cos θ]]

Content:
represents a rotation by an angle [MATH: \theta] counterclockwise about the origin.

Content:
To find the matrix representing a rotation by an angle [MATH: \theta] clockwise about the origin, we replace [MATH: \theta] with [MATH: -\theta] in the above. This gives

Content:
[MATH: [\cos (− θ)|− \sin (− θ); \sin (− θ)|\cos (− θ)]]

---

Item 3 — Example: Rotating a Vector About the Origin

Example Prompt:
The vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}=\langle -5,4 \rangle] is rotated [MATH: 135^{\circ}] counterclockwise about the origin. Find the image of [MATH: \mathbf{v}] under this rotation.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A rotation of [MATH: 135^{\circ}] counterclockwise about the origin is represented by the matrix
[MATH: [\cos (135^{∘})|− \sin (135^{∘}); \sin (135^{∘})|\cos (135^{∘})]]

To find the image [MATH: \mathbf{v}'] under the action of the matrix [MATH: R_{135^{\circ}}], we compute the matrix product, as follows:
[MATH: v^{′}|= R_{135^{∘}} ⋅ v; = [− (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2))][− 5; 4]; = [(1)/(sqrt(2)); − (9)/(sqrt(2))]]

Therefore, the image is [MATH: \mathbf{v}'=\left\langle \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, -\dfrac{9}{\sqrt{2}} \right\rangle.]

Item 6 — Example: Interpreting a Given Matrix as a Rotation

Example Prompt:

[MATH: [− (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2))]]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The rotation matrix [MATH: R_\theta] represents a rotation of angle [MATH: \theta] counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

[MATH: [\cos θ|− \sin θ; \sin θ|\cos θ]]

Comparing [MATH: A] with the rotation matrix, we have

[MATH: {\sin θ = (1)/(sqrt(2)); \cos θ = − (1)/(sqrt(2)).]

Since [MATH: \sin \theta] is positive and [MATH: \cos \theta] is negative, we must have [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \pi.]

Dividing the first equation by the second gives
[MATH: \tan \theta = -1.]

The principal value [MATH: \theta_1] is

[MATH: \theta_1 = \arctan (-1) = -\dfrac{\pi}{4},]

but this is outside the range [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \pi.] To find a value in the required range, we add [MATH: \pi{:}]

[MATH: \theta = \theta_1 + \pi = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}]

Therefore, [MATH: A] represents a rotation of [MATH: \dfrac{3\pi}{4}] radians counterclockwise about the origin.

Note that this is also equivalent to a clockwise rotation with an angle of rotation given by

[MATH: 2\pi - \dfrac{3\pi}{4} = \dfrac{5\pi}{4}.]
